strengths: Genuinely novel paradigm: rendering textual CoT into single-line images and using frozen vision-encoder embeddings as supervision targets for latent reasoning is a new combination of the latent-CoT and text-as-image lines of work, and is well positioned relative to Coconut, CODI, SoftCoT, and CoLaR.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three model architectures (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B), five datasets including OOD and a harder MATH setting, five random seeds with reported 95% CIs, and inference-time measurements on fixed hardware.

Ablations are reasonably thorough and support the design choices: two-stage training (Tab. 2/3), projection-head architecture (Tab. 5), rendering configuration (Tab. 6), decoding strategy (Tab. 4), and a fixed-size-square vs. single-line rendering comparison (Fig. 5). The Stage-I ablation (37.8% vs. 24.8% on GSM8k-Aug) provides evidence that visual supervision is beneficial beyond mere compression.
Good reproducibility posture: code released, LoRA/hyperparameter and special-token initialization details given in the appendix, seeds fixed, validation protocol for MATH specified.
Honest limitations section that acknowledges manual token-budget tuning, decoding instability, restricted domains, and training-time overhead.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'maintaining competitive performance' is overstated. The accuracy gap to explicit CoT is large (37.8% vs. 81.2% on GSM8k-Aug; 33.2% vs. 55.8% on MATH for Qwen3-VL-4B). The efficiency story (Pass@1/#L) is partly by construction: the #L of 32/64 is a hand-fixed hyperparameter, and dynamic termination — the only self-regulating variant — essentially fails (3.87% Pass@1, Tab. 4).

The central 'analyzability / traceability' claim is not actually demonstrated. The paper never decodes generated latent tokens back into images or text to show a human-readable reasoning chain. The evidence is limited to qualitative similarity matrices and heatmaps (Figs. 6–9), which show the opposite problem in Sec. 4.4: latent tokens become nearly homogeneous, suggesting saturation rather than an interpretable step-by-step chain.

The technical alignment in Sec. 3.3.1 is underspecified: rendered CoT produces a variable number of vision patches (image width varies from ~1300px to ~4309px), yet Eq. 1 assumes a one-to-one alignment between step t latent embeddings and K vision embeddings. How the variable-length visual sequence is mapped to the latent token stream, and how many text characters each latent token supervises, is not explained.

The comparison to LLM-based latent baselines (Tab. 2) is not fully controlled: RoT uses Qwen3-VL-4B (with a vision encoder providing extra supervision) while all baselines use Qwen3-4B, so part of the 8.1% gain may come from backbone/data differences rather than the visual-anchor mechanism.

Missing important baselines: explicit CoT with token/length control (e.g., truncated or budget-constrained CoT) at matched inference budgets, and simple text-compression CoT baselines, would clarify whether visual rendering is truly better than cheaper compression at similar token counts.

Restricted scope: only English mathematical reasoning; no commonsense/multilingual tasks, and the practical use case (VLMs that can already read text) leaves the benefit of routing reasoning through the visual encoder somewhat indirect. Small LLaVA results (12.4% on MATH) suggest limited generalization.

strengths: The core idea — rendering textual CoT into images and using frozen vision encoders as semantic anchors for latent reasoning — is a genuinely novel combination of the 'Text-as-Image' and implicit-CoT lines of work, and the paper positions itself well against prior latent reasoning methods (Coconut, CODI, CoLaR).
The two-stage training framework (visual alignment via MSE, then latent supervised fine-tuning with LoRA) is clearly formulated, and ablations confirm both stages contribute (Tab. 2/3).

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: three model architectures, five datasets, five random seeds with 95% CIs, plus ablations on projection-head design, rendering configurations, and decoding strategies.

The paper is transparent about several limitations (task-specific token budgets, dynamic-termination instability, training overhead) and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central accuracy claim is overstated. 'Maintaining competitive performance' is not supported by the evidence: on Qwen3-VL-4B, RoT drops from 81.2% to 37.8% on GSM8k-Aug and from 53.4% to 14.1% on GSM-Hard relative to explicit CoT. The efficiency ratio (Pass@1/#L) masks a severe accuracy degradation; the paper should characterize this honestly as a steep compression-accuracy tradeoff rather than 'competitive'.

The headline motivation — 'Analyzability via Visualization' — is essentially unsupported. The latent tokens are generated without rendering at inference, so the reasoning chain is not actually observable; no method is provided to decode or trace latent tokens back to text. The case studies (Figs. 6–9) are qualitative and speculative ('potentially corresponds to different stages'), and the reported token similarity approaching 1.0 with saturated, homogeneous embeddings actually suggests the opposite of a traceable reasoning chain. The abstract's claim that latent rationales are made 'explicit and traceable' is contradicted by the paper's own analysis.

The mechanistic story is muddled. Rendering text into a 4309px-wide image produces a large number of vision patches, yet the model compresses this into a fixed 32- or 64-token latent budget; the paper does not explain what information survives this bottleneck or why vision-encoder embeddings are better supervision targets than textual/latent alternatives. The claim that 'the visual modality has high information density' driving compression is not analyzed.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: LLM-based latent reasoning baselines (Coconut, CODI, CoLaR) use Qwen3-4B while RoT uses Qwen3-VL-4B, and the closely related Latent Visual Reasoning (Li et al., 2025a) — from which the paper borrows both the instability observation and the special-token initialization — is discussed but not compared as a baseline.

Fixed token budgets are hand-tuned per dataset (32 for GSM8k-Aug, 64 for MATH), and the dynamic-termination alternative collapses (3.87% on GSM8k-Aug), which limits practical deployment; #L of exactly 32.0 across all datasets reflects the fixed budget rather than learned efficiency.

Presentation and citation issues undermine confidence: a citation for GELU is misattributed to Hendrycks (2016); a sentence is duplicated verbatim in Appendix D ('A common pattern observed...'); the introduction claims evaluation on 'logical benchmarks' but only math datasets are used; the case-study prediction 'assistant\n### 2200' is marked correct despite a malformed answer; and the abstract states code availability without an actual URL.

The 'plug-and-play, no additional pre-training' framing is somewhat misleading: Stage I requires dedicated alignment training, and the limitations section concedes extra training-time overhead from rendering and vision encoding.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and well-motivated: using pre-trained vision encoders as frozen semantic anchors to supervise latent reasoning tokens is a clean plug-and-play design that avoids training a reasoning space from scratch, and it is positioned clearly against both token-compression and latent-CoT lines of work.

The two-stage training framework (output-side vision alignment followed by latent SFT) is clearly specified, with equations, architectural details, and special-token initialization described in enough depth (including appendix details on LoRA config, loss weighting, and embedding norms) to support reproduction.

The empirical study is unusually thorough for this paper class: three VLM backbones, five datasets (including OOD and MATH), five seeds with 95% CIs, ablations on both training stages, projection-head architecture, rendering configurations (height/font/padding), and decoding strategies, plus wall-clock inference-time measurements on specified hardware.

The analysis of latent token behavior (similarity matrices, saturation plateau in Sec. 4.4, failure-case patterns in Appendix D) provides some mechanistic insight, and the limitations section is candid about manual token-budget calibration, decoding instability, and training overhead.
weaknesses: The headline 'analyzability / explicit and traceable rationale' claim is largely unsupported. The paper never demonstrates decoding generated latent visual tokens back into images or readable text; at inference, rendering and the vision encoder are discarded, and the 'visualization' amounts to embedding heatmaps and similarity matrices that show statistical structure but not the actual reasoning content. This is the paper's central conceptual claim and the evidence does not substantiate it.

Accuracy degradation relative to explicit CoT is large (e.g., 81.2% to 37.8% on GSM8k-Aug and 53.4% to 14.1% on GSM-Hard for Qwen3-VL-4B), yet the abstract and intro describe the method as 'maintaining competitive performance.' Parity is achieved only on the easiest dataset (MultiArith). The framing overstates what the results show; the honest characterization is a substantial efficiency-accuracy trade-off.

Baseline fairness and validity are questionable. LLM-based baselines are reproduced on Qwen3-4B-Instruct while RoT uses Qwen3-VL-4B, and the reproduced numbers are implausibly low relative to published results (e.g., CODI at 9.7 average accuracy vs. much higher figures in the original work; CoLaR-2 at 40.0 on GSM8k-Aug vs. 81.2 for the authors' own SFT-CoT). This raises doubts that the +8.1% headline improvement over the best LLM-based baseline reflects a real advantage rather than weak reproduction.

The dynamic-termination decoding strategy essentially fails (3.87 Pass@1 on GSM8k-Aug), so the method depends entirely on per-task fixed token budgets tuned on test-informed settings (32 for GSM8k-Aug, 64 for MATH). This weakens both the practical usability claim and the reported '#L' numbers, which are just the fixed budget (32.0±.00) rather than measured usage.

The 'first framework' novelty claim is overstated given the closely related LVR (Li et al., 2025a), which is cited but not differentiated in depth; the delta from that prior work needs sharper articulation.

Reproducibility details are inconsistent: the code URL is a placeholder ('available at' with no link), and the appendix states all random seeds are fixed to 0 for training while the main text reports five random seeds with confidence intervals; the SFT-w/o-CoT rows report #L of 0.00, which is an ill-defined metric.

Possible reporting error: in Fig. 6, the MATH case prediction is '### 2200' while the ground truth is 2220, yet it is marked correct with a green check, which undermines confidence in the qualitative analysis.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel within the implicit-CoT literature: using rendered CoT images and frozen, pre-trained vision encoders as semantic anchors for latent reasoning supervision, rather than learning latent spaces from scratch. This is clearly positioned against Coconut, CODI, CoLaR, SoftCoT, and the 'text-as-image' line (PixelWorld, Glyph), and the 'first to apply visual rendering to compress reasoning steps' claim appears defensible.

The two-stage training framework (visual alignment with a frozen backbone/projection-head-only phase, followed by LoRA-based latent supervised fine-tuning) is well motivated and cleanly specified; equations and implementation details (LoRA config, lambda=10, special-token embedding initialization) support reproducibility.

Broad empirical coverage: five mathematical benchmarks plus GPQA/ProsQA, three VLM backbones (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B), five random seeds with reported confidence intervals, ablations over both training stages, rendering configurations (height/font/padding), projection-head architecture, and decoding strategies.

The authors proactively address a key fairness concern by reproducing LLM-based latent baselines (Coconut, CODI, CoLaR) on a unified Qwen3-VL-4B backbone (Appendix E, Tab. 8), showing gains are not simply due to VLM pretraining.

The analysis sections (token-similarity saturation, failure-case structure, dynamic-termination failure analysis) go beyond pure benchmarking, and limitations/hyperparameter-cost honesty (e.g., 1.5x training time, task-specific budget calibration) is commendable.
Writing and figures are generally clear; the efficiency framing (Pass@1/#L, per-sample latency on a single H20) is a reasonable way to evaluate the compression-accuracy trade-off.
weaknesses: The headline 'maintaining competitive accuracy' claim overstates the evidence: accuracy drops are large on the main training distribution (Qwen3-VL-4B: 81.2% vs 37.8% on GSM8k-Aug; 79.3% vs 55.4% average vs SFT-CoT). Near-parity holds only on the easiest tasks (MultiArith). The contribution is better described as a Pareto trade-off than accuracy preservation, and the paper does not quantify where the trade-off is acceptable.

The central 'analyzability/traceability' motivation is weakly substantiated. At inference no rendering occurs, so the latent chain cannot be decoded back into readable rationale; the 'visualization' evidence (heatmaps, similarity matrices, norm plots) does not reveal reasoning content. The observed homogeneity/saturation of tokens (Sec. 4.4) arguably contradicts the traceability claim rather than supporting it, and Fig. 6's decoded 'trace' (raw 'assistant\n### 2200') is not informative. Notably, the Fig. 6 prediction '### 2200' appears to be a wrong answer (true answer 2220) yet is marked correct with a green check, raising evaluation-quality concerns.

The fixed-token-budget decoding requires task-specific calibration (32 tokens for GSM8k-Aug, 64 for MATH), and it is unclear how these budgets were selected; if chosen on test accuracy (as Tab. 4 suggests), this risks test-set tuning. The more principled dynamic-termination strategy fails catastrophically (3.87 vs 37.8 Pass@1 on GSM8k-Aug), so the practical method reduces to a tuned fixed budget, which weakens both the efficiency claims and the 'self-regulated reasoning' narrative.

Several results invite scrutiny: ProsQA at 100.0 and GPQA at 60.5 with a 4B model compressed to 32-64 latent tokens are surprisingly high, and Tab. 9 lacks an SFT-CoT or w/o-CoT baseline, so generalization claims there are not contextualized. Some odd reporting details (SFT-w/o CoT with #L = 0.00, temperature 1.0/top-p 0.9 for Pass@1 rather than greedy decoding) reduce confidence in the evaluation protocol.

Relationship to LVR (Li et al., 2025a) is underexplored: LVR also performs latent visual reasoning with fixed-budget decoding and exhibits the same termination failure; the paper borrows LVR's initialization and cites its failure mode, but the precise methodological delta beyond rendering-CoT-as-supervision-targets deserves sharper articulation.

The MATH results show RoT barely beats the no-CoT baseline (33.2 vs 29.4), suggesting the method may not yet add real reasoning capability on hard tasks, only slight gains; the paper should confront this more directly.

Minor presentation issues: truncated code link in the abstract, citation formatting errors (e.g., 'D Hendrycks. 2016. Gaussian error linear units' attributed to the wrong work), 'From text to pixel (Lu et al., 2024).' punctuation, and duplicated sentences in Appendix H.

strengths: The core idea—using the frozen vision encoder of a VLM as a semantic anchor to supervise latent reasoning tokens via rendering CoT text into images—is a genuinely different angle on latent CoT compression, and the 'text-to-vision' (output-side) alignment direction is a clean inversion of standard MLLM projection.

The experimental coverage is broad: three base models, four grade-school benchmarks plus MATH, five random seeds with reported CIs, ablations on both training stages, decoding strategies, projection-head architecture, rendering configurations, training cost, and a unified-backbone comparison (Tab. 8) that addresses the otherwise unfair LLM-vs-VLM backbone comparison in Tab. 2.

The paper is transparent about notable weaknesses, including the failure of dynamic termination (Tab. 4), the 1.5× training-time overhead (Tab. 7), and token-budget calibration requirements; fixed seeds and implementation details in Appendix A support reproducibility, and code is stated to be released.
The qualitative analysis of latent tokens (saturation plateau, similarity structure in successful vs. failure cases) is a useful empirical observation about continuous latent reasoning.
The writing and figures are generally clear, and the two-stage training framework is well motivated and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The headline framing overstates the results. The paper claims 'competitive efficiency-accuracy Pareto exploration,' but accuracy drops dramatically versus explicit CoT on Qwen3-VL-4B: 37.8 vs. 81.2 on GSM8k-Aug, 14.1 vs. 53.4 on GSM-Hard, 33.2 vs. 55.8 on MATH. The Pass@1/#L ratio is a favorable metric that obscures this; gains over the no-CoT baseline are often marginal (e.g., SVAMP 72.7 vs. 70.0, MATH 33.2 vs. 29.4). The central efficiency claim is technically true but the 'competitive accuracy' claim is not well supported.

The core 'analyzability/traceability' motivation is not actually delivered. At inference no image is rendered or decoded—the latent tokens are generated directly, so the reasoning chain is as opaque as in Coconut/CODI. The images only serve as training supervision. Worse, Sec. 4.4 and Fig. 6 show the latent tokens become homogeneous and saturate after the initial phase, which actively contradicts the claim that the method makes intermediate reasoning observable and diagnosable.

The method essentially reduces to a fixed-length latent budget: dynamic termination via the special token collapses (3.87 vs. 37.8 on GSM8k-Aug), so the reported 3-4× compression is largely a consequence of truncating the reasoning chain to a tuned constant (32/64 tokens), not of learned, meaningful compression. The mechanism by which 32 latent tokens can represent arbitrarily long rendered CoT (the alignment target K in Eq. 1 varies with text length while the budget is fixed) is underspecified.

Several reported numbers undermine confidence in the evaluation: 100.0 Pass@1 on ProsQA and 60.5 on GPQA (Tab. 9) are not plausible for a 4B model without a strong caveat (possible leakage or train-on-test setup), yet they are presented without scrutiny. Baseline reproductions in Tab. 2 (e.g., CODI at 9.7 average) also look suspiciously low relative to published numbers, and Tab. 2 compares LLM baselines on Qwen3-4B against RoT on Qwen3-VL-4B, with the fair comparison relegated to the appendix.

Novelty over the closely related LVR (Li et al., 2025a) and the text-as-image line (Glyph, PixelWorld, From Text to Pixel) is not sharply delineated; the paper leans on LVR for its decoding failure analysis and initialization scheme, but the incremental delta over LVR is never clearly articulated.

The confidence intervals appear implausibly tight (±0.2-0.4) for generation with temperature 1.0 across five seeds, and the effect sizes on some datasets (MultiArith, SVAMP) are within or near noise, weakening several generalization claims.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated paradigm: rendering textual CoT into single-line images and using the frozen vision encoder of an existing VLM as a supervision anchor for latent reasoning is a creative combination of the implicit-CoT and text-as-image lines of work, with a genuine plug-and-play advantage (no extra pre-training beyond a small projection head and LoRA).

Extensive and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation: three VLM architectures, multiple datasets (GSM8k-Aug, GSM-Hard, SVAMP, MultiArith, MATH), five random seeds with reported confidence intervals, OOD testing, and extension to non-mathematical reasoning (GPQA/ProsQA).

Thorough ablations: two-stage training components, projection-head architecture (activation/dimension), rendering configurations (height/font/padding), decoding strategies (dynamic vs. fixed budgets), and unified-backbone comparison (Appendix E) that partially addresses the base-model confound in Table 2.

Honest reporting of limitations, including the failure of dynamic termination, the need for task-specific token budgets, and higher training cost (Table 7), plus a useful qualitative case study of latent token statistics and failure modes.
The unified-backbone results (Table 8) support the claim that gains come from the method rather than the VLM backbone: RoT outperforms adapted Coconut/CODI/CoLaR baselines on average.
weaknesses: The headline 'analyzability/traceability' claim is only weakly supported. The paper never demonstrates that a latent reasoning chain can be decoded back into rendered images (or otherwise interpreted) to trace the model's rationale or diagnose errors. Section 4.4 actually shows latent tokens become increasingly homogeneous and saturate after an initial phase, which undercuts, rather than supports, the interpretability claim. The visualizations provided are embedding statistics, not readable reasoning traces.

The '3-4x token compression' claim is partly trivial: #L is exactly 32.0±0.00 (or 64.0) across all datasets, i.e., a fixed budget imposed at inference rather than a learned, adaptive compression. The meaningful comparison is the accuracy lost at a given budget, and this loss is substantial (e.g., 55.4 vs. 79.3 average Pass@1 on Qwen3-VL-4B; 37.8 vs. 81.2 on GSM8k-Aug), so the framing as Pareto-competitive with explicit CoT overstates the result.

Positioning relative to the closest prior work, Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR, Li et al., 2025a), is unclear. LVR is cited mainly for the dynamic-termination failure, but the relationship between RoT and LVR (both operate in a visual latent space with fixed-budget decoding) deserves direct empirical comparison and a sharper novelty argument.

Comparison fairness concerns: Table 2 compares a VLM-based method (Qwen3-VL-4B) against LLM-based baselines (Qwen3-4B); the unified-backbone appendix mitigates this but reveals CoLaR-2 still wins on GSM8k-Aug (39.2 vs. 37.8).

Dynamic termination essentially fails (3.87 vs. 37.8 Pass@1), forcing reliance on fixed budgets; this means the method offers no self-regulated reasoning length, limiting the practical value of the paradigm and weakening the efficiency narrative.

Some results appear suspicious or under-explained: #L of 0.00 for SFT-w/o CoT, a perfect 100.0 Pass@1 on ProsQA, and confidence intervals that seem implausibly tight for 5 seeds on ~1k test samples (e.g., ±0.30 on ~80% accuracy). These need clarification for reproducibility.

The efficiency-accuracy trade-off is essentially controlled by a single hyperparameter (token budget) that must be tuned per task; the paper acknowledges this but it limits general applicability and makes cross-method comparisons budget-sensitive.

Reproducibility is promised (code 'available at') but the released material could not be verified; some technical details (e.g., Eqn. 2 notation, the garbled rendering of loss terms) would benefit from clarification.
